title: Philip K. Dick and the Umbrella of Light
author: Angus Taylor
card_summary: Angus Taylor's 'Philip K. Dick and the Umbrella of Light' (T-K Graphics, Baltimore, 1975) — one of the very earliest book-length critical essays on PKD, published in the months immediately following the 2-3-74 events while PKD was still actively writing the Exegesis. Parts had appeared in Foundation (no. 4, July 1973) as 'Can God Fly? Can He Hold Out His Arms and Fly?' Three parts: 'Monsters from Outer and Inner Space,' 'The Willing Extension of Disbelief,' and 'The Umbrella of Light.' Illustrations by C. Lee Healy.
page_summary:
Angus Taylor's Philip K. Dick and the Umbrella of Light (T-K Graphics, Baltimore, 1975) is one of the very earliest book-length critical essays on PKD, predating Robinson's monograph (1984), Mackey's Twayne (1988), Warrick's Mind in Motion (1987), and Sutin's biography (1989) by nearly a decade. It is contemporaneous with PKD's most active period of post-2-3-74 Exegesis writing. The opening epigraph from Blake's 'Auguries of Innocence' ('God Appears & God is Light / To those poor Souls who dwell in Night, / But does a Human Form Display / To those who Dwell in Realms of day') frames the essay's concern with the appearance of the divine in PKD's work.

The text was published as a 33-page chapbook by T-K Graphics in Baltimore — a small fan-academic press that published several early SF critical pamphlets in the mid-1970s. Earlier portions had appeared in the British SF criticism journal Foundation (no. 4, July 1973) as 'Can God Fly? Can He Hold Out His Arms and Fly?' The 1975 expansion is therefore the first sustained statement of Taylor's reading. C. Lee Healy provided illustrations.

Structure: three parts. (1) 'Monsters from Outer and Inner Space' — readings of the early SF novels through the figure of the alien-as-double. (2) 'The Willing Extension of Disbelief' — Taylor's signature inversion of Coleridge's phrase, reading PKD's narrative method as the deliberate refusal of suspension of disbelief in favor of its sustained extension. (3) 'The Umbrella of Light' — the title image from Eye in the Sky (1957) used as a frame for PKD's developing theology of mediated divine appearance.

Contributions to PKD studies: (1) one of the very first book-length critical treatments of PKD; (2) the 'extension of disbelief' formulation has been picked up by later critics (notably echoed in Suvin's cognitive-estrangement program though developed independently); (3) personal-friendship perspective — Taylor was acquainted with PKD and conducted philosophical conversations with him that influenced both Taylor's reading and the Exegesis's Platonic frame; (4) early pre-academic recognition of PKD as a writer of philosophical and theological seriousness.

Position in the literature: contemporary with Lem's 1972 'Visionary Among the Charlatans' (the year the German original appeared) but independent of it; predates the academic-monograph wave (Robinson 1984, Warrick 1987, Mackey 1988) by a decade; sits with Bruce Gillespie's Australian fan-academic monograph Philip K. Dick: Electric Shepherd (1975) as the two earliest book-length PKD critical works. Taylor's confirmation that PKD's philosophy was 'thoroughgoing Platonistic' has been cited in subsequent treatments of PKD's relation to Plato.
